name: Tentorium cerebelli and incisura
summary: A tent-shaped dural fold that roofs the posterior cranial fossa, separating the cerebellum from the occipital lobes and dividing the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments. Its free anterior edge forms the tentorial incisura (notch) through which the midbrain passes, accompanied by the oculomotor nerves, the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and the basal veins. This notch is the site of the herniation syndromes: the uncus herniates down through it and the cerebellar vermis herniates up through it. The transverse sinuses run in its attached margin and the straight sinus along its junction with the falx.

anatomy.location: Attached posteriorly to the transverse sulci of the occipital bone, laterally to the petrous ridges and anteriorly to the clinoid processes; the falx cerebri is attached to its upper surface in the midline; the free edge surrounds the midbrain.

function: Support of the occipital lobes, compartmentalization of pressure between the supratentorial and infratentorial spaces, and housing of the transverse and straight sinuses.

arteries: tentorial branches of the internal carotid (meningohypophyseal trunk)

bestView.label: tentorium separating occipital lobe from cerebellum
tentorium from the straight sinus to the occipital bone; the incisura in front
incisura around the midbrain with the ambient cisterns

imaging.normalAppearance: A dense line sloping from the vertex of the posterior fossa to the petrous ridges on coronal images; on axial CT its edge appears as a V or Y shape and blood along it (tentorial subdural) is common after trauma. The perimesencephalic cisterns at the incisura should be open; their effacement means transtentorial herniation.

pathology.finding: Medial temporal lobe displaced through the incisura with effaced ambient cistern, midbrain compression and a dilated ipsilateral pupil.
Superior vermis pushed through the incisura by a posterior fossa mass, flattening the quadrigeminal cistern.
Dural-based enhancing mass on either surface of the tentorium.
Dense blood along the tentorium after trauma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT for herniation and blood; MRI with contrast for masses

lesionEffects.deficit: Third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil
lesionEffects.mechanism: Uncus compressing the oculomotor nerve at the incisura

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis, or ipsilateral via Kernohan notch
lesionEffects.mechanism: Cerebral peduncle compressed against the tentorial edge
PCA compressed against the tentorial edge
Trochlear nerve running along the free edge

examination: Visual fields after recovery from herniation
pearls: The tentorial notch is where supratentorial pressure meets the brainstem; the blown pupil is its alarm
A patient who survives uncal herniation often wakes with a hemianopia from PCA compression
